issues.item: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
issues.explanation: The threat items imply a trauma context dominated by interpersonal assault or ambush cues (others' sudden movements, ominous silence) rather than toxic chemical exposure. For a chemical exposure trauma, these are hard to reconcile unless there is additional unreported assault/combat context.

issues.item: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
issues.explanation: The negative appraisal about losing connection to community/culture is not well anchored to the rest of the profile. The other selected items center on intrusive memory, overwhelm, and coping incapacity, but there are no related triggers, memories, or strategies suggesting social/cultural disconnection as a core post-trauma theme.

issues.item: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: This item is the least coherent with the rest of the profile. For a 72-year-old married male Coast Guard patient with toxic chemical exposure, the dominant pattern elsewhere is threat, intrusive sensory memory, and low coping around reminders. 'Lost connection to my community and culture' is not impossible, but it is not well supported by the trauma type or by the other selected threat/memory/appraisal items, which center on danger, overwhelm, and inability to handle recall. It reads as a broader social-identity consequence that is disconnected from the active formulation, where Memory and Threat are tightly linked and Negative Appraisals are threat-focused. This makes that individual appraisal item clinically weakly matched to the rest of the self-report.

vignette:
Kofi Osei was 48 years old when the chemical leak erupted from a corroded valve in the engine room of the Coast Guard cutter he served on. As the damage control chief, he was among the first to reach the source, and a cloud of solvent fumes engulfed him before he could seal his mask. He remembers the moment in photographic detail—the hiss of escaping gas, the way the overhead lights seemed to dim, the burning in his lungs that made him think his chest was collapsing. He was evacuated, decontaminated, and medically cleared within a week, but the memory never cleared. It kept returning like a film that played over and over, each time so vivid that he felt the same suffocating pressure. And each time the memory surfaced, he was overcome by emotion—so overwhelmed that he had to stop whatever he was doing, pressing his palms against a wall until the wave passed. He came to believe that if he let himself think about the event at all, he would lose control completely, so he began pushing the thoughts away the instant they started to form. That avoidance felt necessary, but it did nothing to stop the images; they only came more frequently, often when he least expected them.

In the years since, Kofi retired from active duty, but he still volunteers two days a week at the Coast Guard station, helping with orientation tours. The station is familiar, but it no longer feels safe. He has become certain that the world is a dangerous place—every silent corridor, every idle moment between tasks signals that something terrible is about to happen. That belief keeps his vigilance high: at home, he finds himself checking the locks three times before bed; at the station, he scans the faces of visitors for any sign of trouble. Even the ordinary quiet of his living room now feels ominous. When the house falls silent, his muscles tense and his heart speeds up—a physical reactivity that tells him danger is near. And in those moments of hypervigilance, the memory of the chemical cloud often rises unbidden, as if his body is reliving the exposure all over again. The connection between feeling threatened and remembering the event has become automatic: the more on guard he feels, the more the memory intrudes, and the more the memory intrudes, the more dangerous the world seems.

Kofi’s daily life has narrowed. He avoids the engineering section of the station where the smell of fuel oil sometimes drifts, and he will not enter hardware stores because cleaning products trigger the same burning sensation in his throat. At home, his wife, Grace, has noticed he no lingers in the kitchen when she uses bleach; he stays in the bedroom with the door closed. The worst moments come during silence. At a recent family dinner, the table fell quiet as everyone ate, and Kofi felt his chest tighten so sharply that he excused himself and stood in the backyard until the feeling passed. He told Grace it was nothing, but he was certain he could not handle even the slightest upset anymore—that his ability to cope had evaporated completely. That belief feeds back into his vigilance: because he believes he is fragile, he stays alert for anything that might disturb his composure, and that alertness only makes him feel more exhausted and inadequate. The cycle has left him feeling trapped in his own home.

What finally brought Kofi to seek help was an incident at the station last month. A fire drill siren went off, and within seconds he was drenched in sweat, his hands trembling, the photographic image of the chemical cloud filling his mind. He had to sit down on a bench and asked a colleague to get him water. The young volunteer who helped him looked worried, and Kofi realized that his reactions were becoming visible to others. Grace had been urging him to see someone for over a year, but he had resisted because he was afraid that talking about the event would make it worse—that he would not be able to handle the memories if he let himself speak them aloud. Now he has come to the clinic hoping to find a way to stop the constant scanning, to sit through a quiet room without his heart racing. But underneath that hope is a deeper fear: that he may already be too fragile to change, and that the world he once navigated with steady hands will never feel safe again.
